exampleAnswers.title: Understanding the Even Extension of a Function

question.text: Let $F(x)=xe^{x}$ for $x\in[0,\pi),$ and let $f(x)$ be the even extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-\pi,\pi).$ What is the value of $f(-2)?$
question.explanation:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,\pi),$ the even extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} F(x), & x\in[0,\pi), \\[5pt] F(-x), & x\in(-\pi,0). \end{cases} \]

In our case, for $x\in(-\pi,0),$ we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= F(-x) \\[5pt] &= (-x)e^{-x} \\[5pt] &= -xe^{-x}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align*} f(-2) &= -(-2)e^{-(-2)} = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{2e^2}. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $F(x)=x^2-2x$ for $x\in[0,\pi),$ and let $f(x)$ be the even extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-\pi,\pi).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in(-\pi,0)?$
question.explanation:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,\pi),$ the even extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} F(x), & x\in[0,\pi), \\[5pt] F(-x), & x\in(-\pi,0). \end{cases} \]

In our case, for $x\in(-\pi,0),$ we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= F(-x) \\[5pt] &= (-x)^2-2(-x) \\[5pt] &= x^2+2x. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $F(x)=x^2e^{x^2}$ for $x\in[0,\pi),$ and let $f(x)$ be the even extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-\pi,\pi).$ What is the value of $f(-3)?$
question.explanation:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,\pi),$ the even extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} F(x), & x\in[0,\pi), \\[5pt] F(-x), & x\in(-\pi,0). \end{cases} \]

In our case, for $x\in(-\pi,0),$ we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= F(-x) \\[5pt] &= (-x)^2e^{(-x)^2} \\[5pt] &= x^2e^{x^2}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \begin{align*} f(-3) &= (-3)^2e^{(-3)^2} = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{9e^9}. \end{align*}

question.text: Let $F(x)=3e^x+x$ for $x\in[0,\pi),$ and let $f(x)$ be the even extension of $F(x)$ to $x \in (-\pi,\pi).$ What is $f(x)$ for $x\in(-\pi,0)?$
question.explanation:
If $F(x)$ is defined on $x\in[0,\pi),$ the even extension of $F$ is the function $f$ such that \[ f(x) = \begin{cases} F(x), & x\in[0,\pi), \\[5pt] F(-x), & x\in(-\pi,0). \end{cases} \]

In our case, for $x\in(-\pi,0),$ we get \begin{align*} f(x) &= F(-x) \\[5pt] &= 3e^{(-x)}+(-x) \\[5pt] &= 3e^{-x}-x. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing the Constant Term From the Half-Range Formula

question.text: \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos(nx) \] Let $F(x)=3x^2+2$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ The Fourier cosine series of the even $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for $a_0.$
question.explanation:
For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by \[ a_0=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=3x^2+2$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get \begin{align*} a_0 &= \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (3x^2+2) \,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left[ x^3+2x \right]_{0}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} (\pi^3+2\pi) - 0 \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{2(\pi^2+2)}. \end{align*}

question.text: \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos(nx) \] Let $F(x)=5x^2+1$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ The Fourier cosine series of the even $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for $a_0.$
question.explanation:
For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by \[ a_0=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=5x^2+1$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get \begin{align*} a_0 &= \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (5x^2+1) \,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left[ \dfrac{5x^3}{3}+x \right]_{0}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left(\dfrac{5\pi^3}{3}+\pi\right) - 0 \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{2\left(\dfrac{5\pi^2}{3}+1\right)}. \end{align*}

example.title: Computing the Constant Term From the Half-Range Formula

question.text: \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos(nx) \] Let $F(x)=-\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{6}\right)$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ The Fourier cosine series of the even $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for $a_0.$
question.explanation:
For our Fourier cosine series, the constant term is given by \[ a_0=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=-\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{6}\right)$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get \begin{align*} a_0 &= \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi -\sin\left(\dfrac{x}{6}\right) \,\text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left[ 6\cos\left(\dfrac{x}{6}\right) \right]_{0}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left( 6\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{6}\right) - 6\cos(0) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left( 6\cdot \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} - 6\right) \\[5pt] &= \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{6(\sqrt{3}-2)}{\pi}}. \end{align*}

exampleAnswers.title: Computing the Cosine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula

question.text: Let $F(x)=2x+3$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the even $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.
question.explanation:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by \[ a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\cos(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=2x+3$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get \[ a_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (2x+3) \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

We use the integration by parts: \begin{align*} u=2x+3 \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad u' = 2 \\[3pt] v' = \cos(nx) \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad v = \dfrac{1}{n}\sin(nx) \end{align*}

Thus, we obtain \begin{align*} a_n &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left( uv\,\Big|_0^\pi - \int_0^\pi vu' \,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left( \dfrac{1}{n} \big[ (2x+3)\sin(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} - \dfrac{2}{n} \int_0^\pi \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{n\pi} \left( \left( (2\pi+3)\sin(n\pi) - 3\sin(0) \right) + \dfrac{2}{n} \big[ \cos(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{n\pi} \left( 0+ \dfrac{2}{n} \left( \cos(n\pi)-\cos(0) \right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{4(\cos(n\pi)-1)}{n^2\pi}. \end{align*}

Therefore, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have \[ a_n = \dfrac{4((-1)^n-1)}{\pi n^2}. \]

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is \[ f(x) \sim (3+\pi) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{4((-1)^n-1)}{\pi n^2}} \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\cos(nx)}. \]

example.title: Computing the Cosine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula

question.text: \[ f(x) \sim \dfrac{a_0}{2} + \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n \cos(nx) \] Let $F(x)=-4x$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ The Fourier cosine series of the even $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of $F(x)$ is shown above. Find the expression for $a_n.$
question.explanation:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by \[ a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\cos(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=-4x$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get \[ a_n = -\dfrac{8}{\pi}\int_0^\pi x \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

We use the integration by parts: \begin{align*} u=x \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad u' = 1 \\[3pt] v' = \cos(nx) \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad v = \dfrac{1}{n}\sin(nx) \end{align*}

Thus, we obtain \begin{align*} a_n &= -\dfrac{8}{\pi} \left( uv\,\Big|_0^\pi - \int_0^\pi vu' \,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{8}{\pi} \left( \dfrac{1}{n} \big[ x\sin(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} - \dfrac{1}{n} \int_0^\pi \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{8}{n\pi} \left( \left( \pi\cdot\sin(n\pi) - 0\cdot\sin(0) \right) + \dfrac{1}{n} \big[ \cos(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} \right) \\[5pt] &= -\dfrac{8}{n\pi} \left( 0+ \dfrac{1}{n} \left( \cos(n\pi)-\cos(0) \right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8(1-\cos(n\pi))}{n^2\pi}. \end{align*}

Finally, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have \[ a_n = \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{8(1-(-1)^n)}{\pi n^2}}. \]

example.title: Computing the Cosine Coefficients From the Half-Range Formula

question.text: Let $F(x)=7x-4$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the even $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.
question.explanation:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by \[ a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\cos(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=7x-4$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get \[ a_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (7x-4) \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

We use the integration by parts: \begin{align*} u=7x-4 \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad u' = 7 \\[3pt] v' = \cos(nx) \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad v = \dfrac{1}{n}\sin(nx) \end{align*}

Thus, we obtain \begin{align*} a_n &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left( uv\,\Big|_0^\pi - \int_0^\pi vu' \,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left( \dfrac{1}{n} \big[ (7x-4)\sin(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} - \dfrac{7}{n} \int_0^\pi \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{n\pi} \left( \left( (7\pi-4)\sin(n\pi) + 4\sin(0) \right) + \dfrac{7}{n} \big[ \cos(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{n\pi} \left( 0+ \dfrac{7}{n} \left( \cos(n\pi)-\cos(0) \right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{14(\cos(n\pi)-1)}{n^2\pi}. \end{align*}

Therefore, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have \[ a_n = \dfrac{14((-1)^n-1)}{\pi n^2}. \]

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is \[ f(x) \sim \left(-4+\dfrac{7\pi}{2}\right) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{14((-1)^n-1)}{\pi n^2}} \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\cos(nx)}. \]

question.text: Let $F(x)=4x-1$ for $x\in[0,\pi).$ Select the correct missing parts in the Fourier cosine series of the even $2\pi$-periodic extension $f(x)$ of the function $F(x)$ below.
question.explanation:
For our Fourier cosine series, the coefficients are given by \[ a_n=\frac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi f(x)\cos(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

In our case, $f(x)=4x-1$ for $x \in (0,\pi).$ So, substituting into the formula, we get \[ a_n = \dfrac{2}{\pi}\int_0^\pi (4x-1) \cos(nx)\,\text{d}x. \]

We use the integration by parts: \begin{align*} u=4x-1 \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad u' = 4 \\[3pt] v' = \cos(nx) \qquad&\Rightarrow\qquad v = \dfrac{1}{n}\sin(nx) \end{align*}

Thus, we obtain \begin{align*} a_n &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left( uv\,\Big|_0^\pi - \int_0^\pi vu' \,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{\pi} \left( \dfrac{1}{n} \big[ (4x-1)\sin(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} - \dfrac{4}{n} \int_0^\pi \sin(nx)\,\text{d}x \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{n\pi} \left( \left( (4\pi-1)\sin(n\pi) + \sin(0) \right) + \dfrac{4}{n} \big[ \cos(nx) \big]_{0}^{\pi} \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{2}{n\pi} \left( 0+ \dfrac{4}{n} \left( \cos(n\pi)-\cos(0) \right) \right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{8(\cos(n\pi)-1)}{n^2\pi}. \end{align*}

Therefore, since $\cos(n\pi)=(-1)^n,$ we have \[ a_n = \dfrac{8((-1)^n-1)}{\pi n^2}. \]

Finally, the Fourier cosine series is \[ f(x) \sim (-1+2\pi) + \sum_{n=1}^\infty \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\dfrac{8((-1)^n-1)}{\pi n^2}} \cdot \bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\cos(nx)}. \]
